etymology: From twelve, one chosen of each tribe; spy from Old French espier, to watch or search out, rendering Hebrew tur, to search out the land (Numbers 13:2).
biblical_def: The twelve men, a ruler of every tribe, whom Moses sent from Kadesh-barnea to search out the land of Canaan (Num 13:1-3). They returned after forty days bearing the fruit of the land, and all confessed the land was good and flowed with milk and honey. But ten brought up an evil report of the land, saying, "We be not able to go up against the people; for they are stronger than we" (Num 13:31), and so they discouraged the heart of the people. Only Caleb and Joshua believed the word of the LORD and stilled the people, saying, "Let us go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it" (Num 13:30). The congregation lifted up their voice and wept, murmured against Moses and Aaron, and sought to make a captain to return into Egypt. For this unbelief the LORD swore that not one of that generation, save Caleb and Joshua, should see the land; their carcases fell in the wilderness, and the ten faithless spies died of the plague before the LORD (Num 14:36-37). The episode is a fixed type of the rest of God forfeited through unbelief and hardness of heart (Heb 3:7-4:11). This dictionary confesses that the land was lost not for want of power in God but for want of faith in man, and that the same gospel which was preached unto them must be mixed with faith in them that hear it.
webster_summary: The twelve men sent by Moses to search out Canaan. Ten returned with an evil report and bred unbelief; Caleb and Joshua trusted the LORD's promise. The faithless generation was barred from the land.
webster_full: TWELVE SPIES, noun. The twelve rulers, one of each tribe, whom Moses sent to search the land of Canaan from the wilderness of Paran.
"And Moses by the commandment of the LORD sent them from the wilderness of Paran: all those men were heads of the children of Israel" (Num 13:3).
Their report required of them faith in the promise of God who had given the land.
Ten denied that faith and discouraged the people; two, Caleb and Joshua, confessed it and were preserved.
The sanction: that generation perished in the wilderness, a standing warning against unbelief.
scriptures: And Caleb stilled the people before Moses, and said, Let us go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it.
But the men that went up with him said, We be not able to go up against the people; for they are stronger than we.
Num 14:9
Only rebel not ye against the LORD, neither fear ye the people of the land; for they are bread for us: their defence is departed from them, and the LORD is with us: fear them not.
Heb 3:19
So we see that they could not enter in because of unbelief.
corruption_summary: There is no postmodern redefinition of the spies; the standing peril is the unbelief that hears the promise of God and shrinks from it.
corruption_paragraphs: The error of the ten was not in seeing the giants and the walled cities; Caleb and Joshua saw the same. The error was to weigh the visible strength of the enemy against nothing, when they ought to have weighed it against the word and arm of the LORD who had divided the sea and fed them with bread from heaven. Unbelief is never a sober realism; it is a forgetting of God, and it spreads like a plague through a congregation until the whole assembly weeps to return to Egypt.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The positive principle to recover is that the promises of God are made good only to faith, and that the report of the present world's strength must always be heard under the louder report of God's covenant faithfulness. The believer is called to be of Caleb's mind, who wholly followed the LORD, and so to enter the rest that the murmurers forfeited.
roots_summary: From Hebrew tur, to search out or explore, the verb used of the spies searching the land of Canaan.
roots_lines: Hebrew tur (Num 13:2) means to search out, explore, or spy out a land.
Each spy was a nasi, a ruler or prince of his father's tribe.
The land was searched forty days, answering to the forty years of wandering decreed for the forty days.
An "evil report" renders dibbah, a slander or whispering against the land God praised.
Caleb's name is joined ever after to the phrase "wholly followed the LORD" (Num 14:24).
usage: The sermon on the twelve spies pressed home that unbelief, not the giants, kept Israel from Canaan.
Like Caleb among the twelve spies, the saint reckons the enemy as bread before the presence of God.
The murmuring that the twelve spies stirred up became the pattern of every wilderness rebellion that followed.

etymology: Hebrew El'azar, "God hath helped," from el (God) and azar (to help); third son of Aaron and his successor in the high priesthood.
biblical_def: Eleazar was the third son of Aaron the high priest (Exod 6:23), set over the charge of the sanctuary and its holy things (Num 3:32; 4:16). When Nadab and Abihu died before the LORD for offering strange fire, Eleazar and Ithamar succeeded their elder brothers in the priest's office (Num 3:4). At the death of Aaron in mount Hor, the LORD commanded Moses to strip Aaron of the high-priestly garments and to put them upon Eleazar his son; and Aaron died there, and Eleazar was invested as high priest in his room (Num 20:25-28). Thenceforth Eleazar stood beside Moses and after him beside Joshua, and it was by the judgment of Eleazar inquiring with the Urim that Israel was to go out and come in (Num 27:21). With Joshua he oversaw the dividing of the inheritance among the tribes by lot (Josh 14:1; 17:4), and he was buried in a hill that pertained to Phinehas his son (Josh 24:33). Eleazar represents the faithful continuance of the Aaronic priestly line, the office passing not by the will of man but by the appointment of God from father to son. This dictionary confesses that the whole Levitical priesthood, Eleazar and all his house, was a shadow of the one great High Priest, Christ Jesus, whose priesthood is unchangeable and who ever liveth to make intercession (Heb 7:24-25).
webster_summary: Aaron's third son, invested with the high-priestly garments at his father's death on mount Hor. He divided the land with Joshua and held the faithful priestly line.
webster_full: ELEAZAR, noun. Son of Aaron, succeeding him as high priest of Israel; the name signifies "God hath helped."
"And Moses stripped Aaron of his garments, and put them upon Eleazar his son; and Aaron died there in the top of the mount" (Num 20:28).
His office required the keeping of the sanctuary and the inquiry by Urim before the LORD.
With Joshua he divided the land of Canaan to the tribes for an inheritance.
He stands as a figure of the continuing priesthood, fulfilled in the unchangeable priesthood of Christ.
scriptures: And Moses stripped Aaron of his garments, and put them upon Eleazar his son; and Aaron died there in the top of the mount: and Moses and Eleazar came down from the mount.

And he shall stand before Eleazar the priest, who shall ask counsel for him after the judgment of Urim before the LORD: at his word shall they go out, and at his word they shall come in, both he, and all the children of Israel with him, even all the congregation.
Josh 14:1

And these are the countries which the children of Israel inherited in the land of Canaan, which Eleazar the priest, and Joshua the son of Nun, and the heads of the fathers of the tribes of the children of Israel, distributed for inheritance to them.
Josh 24:33
And Eleazar the son of Aaron died; and they buried him in a hill that pertained to Phinehas his son, which was given him in mount Ephraim.
corruption_summary: Eleazar faces no modern redefinition; his life recovers the truth that the priestly office is a divine appointment, not a human ambition.
corruption_paragraphs: The investiture on mount Hor teaches that no man taketh the high-priestly honour unto himself; Eleazar received the garments from his father's body only at the express command of God, by the hand of Moses. The orderly passing of the office from Aaron to Eleazar to Phinehas shows that God maintains His own ordinances across generations, and that the failure of Nadab and Abihu did not overthrow the line but only purged it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity and the limits of an office that God Himself institutes. Eleazar held real authority, yet only as a servant of a typical and passing covenant; the believer learns to honour lawful office while resting wholly on the one Mediator whose priesthood needs no successor.
roots_summary: From Hebrew El'azar, "God hath helped," the name of Aaron's son and successor in the high priesthood.
roots_lines: Hebrew El'azar joins el, God, with azar, to help or succour.
The garments "put upon" Eleazar signified the transfer of the whole high-priestly office.
His charge over "the oil for the light" and the holy things marked him as overseer of the sanctuary (Num 4:16).
Inquiry "by Urim" was the lawful means of seeking the LORD's direction through the priest.
His son Phinehas continued the line, knit to a covenant of an everlasting priesthood (Num 25:13).
usage: At Aaron's death Eleazar the priest received the breastplate and ephod and went down from the mount as high priest.
Joshua sought the word of God through Eleazar the priest, who inquired after the judgment of Urim.
The land was parted among the tribes by Eleazar the priest and Joshua at the door of the tabernacle.

etymology: Wilderness from Old English wilddeoren, place of wild beasts; wander from Old English wandrian, to roam; rendering the forty years Israel was made to wander in the desert (Num 32:13).
biblical_def: The forty years during which the generation that came out of Egypt was made to wander in the wilderness of Sinai and Paran until their carcases were consumed, the LORD's judgment upon their unbelief at Kadesh-barnea (Num 14:33-34). For their refusal to enter Canaan He swore, "after the number of the days in which ye searched the land, even forty days, each day for a year, shall ye bear your iniquities, even forty years" (Num 14:34). Yet the wandering was not bare judgment; through all those years God did not forsake His people. He fed them with manna morning by morning, brought water out of the rock, kept their raiment from waxing old and their feet from swelling (Deut 8:4), and went before them in the pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night. He humbled them and proved them, to do them good at their latter end (Deut 8:2-3). The years in the wilderness are therefore the fixed scriptural type of the Christian pilgrimage between redemption and rest, wherein the redeemed are sustained by daily provision, tried in their faith, and warned not to fall after the same example of unbelief (1 Cor 10:1-12). This dictionary confesses that the same God who chastens His people in the way also feeds them every step of it, and that He brings none out of Egypt whom He will finally leave in the desert.
webster_summary: The forty years Israel wandered in the desert under judgment for unbelief, yet daily fed and led by God. A type of the Christian pilgrimage to the promised rest.
webster_full: WILDERNESS WANDERING, noun. The forty years Israel passed in the desert after refusing to enter Canaan at Kadesh-barnea.
"And your children shall wander in the wilderness forty years, and bear your whoredoms, until your carcases be wasted in the wilderness" (Num 14:33).
It required of the people both submission to chastening and trust in daily provision.
God forbade the unbelieving generation entrance, yet fed them with manna and led them by the cloud.
The sense closing: a pattern of the saint's journey from redemption to the rest of God.
scriptures: And your children shall wander in the wilderness forty years, and bear your whoredoms, until your carcases be wasted in the wilderness.
After the number of the days in which ye searched the land, even forty days, each day for a year, shall ye bear your iniquities, even forty years, and ye shall know my breach of promise.
Deut 8:2

And thou shalt remember all the way which the LORD thy God led thee these forty years in the wilderness, to humble thee, and to prove thee, to know what was in thine heart, whether thou wouldest keep his commandments, or no.
Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come.
corruption_summary: The wandering faces no postmodern redefinition; its lesson is the recovery of God's faithfulness in chastening and His daily sustaining of a pilgrim people.
corruption_paragraphs: The wilderness was at once a place of judgment and a place of mercy, and Scripture will not let us divide the two. The same forty years that buried a faithless generation also saw the manna fall without fail and the cloud abide without departing. To read the wandering only as punishment is to forget the kindness woven through it; to read it only as God's provision is to forget the holiness that would not pass over unbelief. The apostle binds both together for our admonition.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the doctrine of the pilgrim church, sustained yet tried, chastened yet kept. The believer travels a desert between his redemption from sin and his entrance into rest, eating the bread of heaven daily and warned by the carcases in the sand not to harden his heart as in the provocation.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew accounts of Israel made to wander (nua, to totter or stray) forty years in the midbar, the wilderness.
roots_lines: Hebrew midbar, wilderness, is the uncultivated waste through which Israel journeyed.
The verb nua, to wander or totter, marks an unsettled and homeless walking.
"Forty" recurs as the scriptural measure of testing, set day-for-year against the forty days of spying.
Manna, "what is it?" (Exod 16:15), names the daily bread that sustained the wandering.
The pillar of cloud and fire was the abiding sign of God's presence in the waste.
usage: The wilderness wandering proves that God chastens His own without ever ceasing to feed them.
Preachers liken the present life to the wilderness wandering, a pilgrimage to a rest not yet entered.
Throughout the wilderness wandering the manna fell six mornings and rested the seventh, teaching the sabbath.

etymology: Hebrew Ba'al Pe'or, "lord of Peor," the Baal worshipped at mount Peor in Moab; baal meaning lord or master, joined to the place-name Peor.
biblical_def: The idol and the apostasy of Israel at Shittim on the plains of Moab, recorded in Numbers 25. While Israel abode there, the people began to commit whoredom with the daughters of Moab, who called them to the sacrifices of their gods; and the people did eat, and bowed down to their gods, "and Israel joined himself unto Baal-peor" (Num 25:3). This was the snare devised by Balaam, who taught Balak to cast a stumblingblock before Israel through Midianite and Moabite seduction (Num 31:16; Rev 2:14). The anger of the LORD was kindled, and a plague went out among the people. It was stayed only when Phinehas the son of Eleazar rose up in holy zeal and thrust through the man of Israel and the Midianitish woman in the very act, turning away the wrath of God; yet there died in the plague twenty and four thousand (Num 25:7-9). Baal-peor became a byword in Israel for that joining of fornication and idolatry which provokes the LORD to jealousy. The Psalmist remembers it: "They joined themselves also unto Baal-peor, and ate the sacrifices of the dead" (Psa 106:28), and Paul holds it up as a warning against fornication and tempting Christ (1 Cor 10:8). This dictionary confesses that idolatry and immorality are sisters, that God is a jealous God who will not give His glory to another, and that the zeal of Phinehas, not the indulgence of the people, is counted to him for righteousness.
webster_summary: The Moabite Baal to which Israel joined itself at Shittim through fornication and sacrifice. A plague slew twenty-four thousand, stayed by the zeal of Phinehas.
webster_full: BAAL-PEOR, noun. The Baal worshipped at mount Peor in Moab, to which Israel joined itself in the apostasy at Shittim.
"And Israel joined himself unto Baal-peor: and the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel" (Num 25:3).
The worship required fornication with the daughters of Moab and eating of the sacrifices of their gods.
It forbids any joining of the LORD's people to the idols and immoralities of the nations.
The sanction: a plague of twenty-four thousand, turned away only by the zeal of Phinehas.
scriptures: Num 25:3
And Israel joined himself unto Baal-peor: and the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel.
Num 25:9
And those that died in the plague were twenty and four thousand.
They joined themselves also unto Baal-peor, and ate the sacrifices of the dead.
Neither let us commit fornication, as some of them committed, and fell in one day three and twenty thousand.
corruption_summary: The sin of Baal-peor is the abiding pattern of idolatry wedded to immorality; it faces no postmodern excuse, only a standing warning to the church.
corruption_paragraphs: The strategy of Balaam, where cursing failed, was to corrupt; he could not curse whom God had blessed, so he counselled seduction. The lesson is that the deadliest assault upon the people of God is not the open foe but the inviting daughter of Moab, the friendship with the world that draws the heart to bow at a strange altar. Fornication and idolatry stand together at Peor because both are a forsaking of the covenant Husband for another lord.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the jealousy of God and the necessity of holy zeal. Phinehas is no model for private vengeance, but his act, executed by a priest under the very judgment of God, was counted for righteousness and stayed the plague. The church recovers him rightly by refusing every Baal-peor of compromise, mortifying the besetting sin that would join her to the world's sacrifices.
roots_summary: From Hebrew Ba'al Pe'or, "lord of Peor," naming the false god of the mountain where Israel sinned at Shittim.
roots_lines: Baal means lord, master, or husband, the common title of the Canaanite storm-deities.
Peor is the mountain in Moab from whose top Balaam had looked upon Israel (Num 23:28).
Shittim, "the acacias," was the last camp of Israel before crossing Jordan (Num 25:1).
The plague answered the breach of the covenant, kindling the anger of a jealous God.
Phinehas' zeal earned a covenant of peace and an everlasting priesthood (Num 25:12-13).
usage: Paul invokes Baal-peor to warn the Corinthians against fornication and the tempting of Christ.
The apostasy at Baal-peor shows how idolatry and immorality forever travel together.
Like the plague at Baal-peor, unchecked compromise spreads death through a careless congregation.

etymology: Hebrew Ebyathar, "father of abundance" or "my father is great," from ab (father) and yathar (to be abundant, to remain over).
biblical_def: Abiathar was the son of Ahimelech the priest of Nob, and the sole survivor of the slaughter that Saul commanded when Doeg the Edomite fell upon the priests for having aided David (1 Sam 22:18-20). Abiathar escaped and fled to David, bringing with him the ephod, and David said unto him, "Abide thou with me, fear not" (1 Sam 22:23). Through David's wilderness years Abiathar inquired of the LORD for him by the ephod, and he shared David's exile and his enthronement, bearing the ark and standing as priest in Jerusalem alongside Zadok. Yet at the last, when Adonijah exalted himself to be king against the LORD's purpose for Solomon, Abiathar took Adonijah's part (1 Kings 1:7). For this Solomon thrust him out from being priest unto the LORD, sparing his life for his faithfulness in David's afflictions, but removing him to his fields at Anathoth (1 Kings 2:26-27). In this the Scripture marks a solemn fulfilment: "that he might fulfil the word of the LORD, which he spake concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh" (1 Kings 2:27), for Abiathar was of Eli's line, and the sentence pronounced against that house was at last accomplished. This dictionary confesses that the word of the LORD standeth sure though it tarry many generations, that long faithfulness does not license a final treason, and that God removes and sets up whom He will, even in the highest offices of His house.
webster_summary: The one priest of Nob who escaped Saul's slaughter and fled to David, serving as his priest. He later sided with Adonijah and was deposed by Solomon, fulfilling the word against Eli's house.
webster_full: ABIATHAR, noun. Son of Ahimelech, priest of Nob; sole escapee of Saul's massacre and high priest under David.
"And one of the sons of Ahimelech the son of Ahitub, named Abiathar, escaped, and fled after David" (1 Sam 22:20).
His office required faithful inquiry of the LORD for the king by the ephod.
He served David long, yet later sided with Adonijah against Solomon, the LORD's chosen.
The sanction: deposed from the priesthood, fulfilling the word spoken against the house of Eli.
scriptures: And one of the sons of Ahimelech the son of Ahitub, named Abiathar, escaped, and fled after David.
Abide thou with me, fear not: for he that seeketh my life seeketh thy life: but with me thou shalt be in safeguard.
1 Kings 2:26

And unto Abiathar the priest said the king, Get thee to Anathoth, unto thine own fields; for thou art worthy of death: but I will not at this time put thee to death, because thou barest the ark of the Lord GOD before David my father, and because thou hast been afflicted in all wherein my father was afflicted.
1 Kings 2:27
So Solomon thrust out Abiathar from being priest unto the LORD; that he might fulfil the word of the LORD, which he spake concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh.
corruption_summary: Abiathar faces no modern redefinition; his fall recovers the truth that long service cannot purchase a final rebellion, and that God's word against a house is sure.
corruption_paragraphs: Abiathar's life is a sober mingling of fidelity and failure. He bore the ark, suffered exile, and inquired faithfully for David through years of danger; no man could question his loyalty in the day of trouble. Yet at the end he chose the wrong king, casting his lot with Adonijah's self-exaltation rather than with Solomon whom the LORD had named. His mercy from Solomon's hand was real, but so was his removal.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the word of the LORD, here the sentence on Eli's house spoken generations before, comes infallibly to pass. A man may serve God's anointed long and still forfeit his office by a late treason; perseverance is proved at the end, not merely begun at the start. God's purposes for His true King will not be overthrown by any priest's misjudgment.
roots_summary: From Hebrew Ebyathar, "father of abundance," the priest who survived Nob and served David.
roots_lines: Hebrew Ebyathar joins ab, father, with the root yathar, to remain over or abound.
He carried the ephod, the priestly garment used to inquire of the LORD.
Of the house of Eli through Ahitub, he stood under the ancient sentence on that line.
Anathoth, his place of banishment, was a Levitical city in Benjamin (Josh 21:18).
Zadok his colleague held the office that passed wholly to his line after Abiathar fell.
usage: Abiathar alone escaped the sword of Doeg and fled with the ephod to David in the cave.
When Adonijah seized the kingdom, Abiathar followed and helped him, to his own undoing.
Solomon's deposing of Abiathar fulfilled to the letter the word long before spoken against Eli.

etymology: Rendering Hebrew gibborim, mighty ones or men of valour, from gabar, to be strong or to prevail; the captains and warriors gathered to David.
biblical_def: The roll of valiant men who gathered to David and wrought his great deliverances, named and numbered in 2 Samuel 23:8-39 and 1 Chronicles 11. They are reckoned in companies of honour: first "the three" mightiest, Adino, Eleazar the son of Dodo, and Shammah, who stood their ground when the people fled and whom the LORD wrought a great victory by (2 Sam 23:9-12); then a second order of valiant men; and "the thirty" among whom were Abishai, Benaiah who slew the lion in the pit in time of snow, and many more, ending with Uriah the Hittite. Their valour was not mere prowess but loyalty knit to the LORD's anointed; gathering first to David in the cave of Adullam when he was an outlaw, they bound their lives to his cause. The chief sign of this is the water of Bethlehem: when David longed for it and three of the mighty men brake through the host of the Philistines to fetch it, David would not drink it, but poured it out unto the LORD, saying it was the blood of the men that went in jeopardy of their lives (2 Sam 23:16-17). This dictionary confesses that such valour, spent for the king and poured out before the LORD, is a shadow of the loyalty owed to Christ the greater David, and that the truly mighty are those who hazard themselves for the Anointed and lay their offerings before God.
webster_summary: The gibborim, the valiant warriors gathered to David, ranked as the three and the thirty. Their valour was bound to covenant loyalty toward the LORD's anointed.
webster_full: MIGHTY MEN, noun plural. The valiant warriors, the gibborim, who gathered to David and wrought his deliverances.
"These be the names of the mighty men whom David had" (2 Sam 23:8).
Their office required valour in battle joined to loyalty toward the LORD's anointed king.
They are ranked as the three, the second order, and the thirty, each named for honour.
The closing sense: valour poured out unto the LORD, as David poured out the water of Bethlehem.
scriptures: These be the names of the mighty men whom David had: The Tachmonite that sat in the seat, chief among the captains; the same was Adino the Eznite: he lift up his spear against eight hundred, whom he slew at one time.

And the three mighty men brake through the host of the Philistines, and drew water out of the well of Bethlehem, that was by the gate, and took it, and brought it to David: nevertheless he would not drink thereof, but poured it out unto the LORD.

And he said, Be it far from me, O LORD, that I should do this: is not this the blood of the men that went in jeopardy of their lives? therefore he would not drink it. These things did these three mighty men.

These also are the chief of the mighty men whom David had, who strengthened themselves with him in his kingdom, and with all Israel, to make him king, according to the word of the LORD concerning Israel.
corruption_summary: The mighty men face no postmodern redefinition; their record recovers the bond of valour and covenant loyalty owed to the LORD's anointed.
corruption_paragraphs: The catalogue of the mighty men is no mere muster-roll of strong arms; it is a record of devotion. These men strengthened themselves with David in his kingdom to make him king according to the word of the LORD. Their feats, slaying hundreds, standing alone in a barley field, leaping into a pit against a lion in the snow, are recorded not to glorify violence but to honour men who hazarded all for the cause of God's chosen king.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that true might is loyalty unto the Anointed, and that the worthiest service is offered up to God. David's pouring out of the hard-won water teaches that what is gotten by the jeopardy of faithful men belongs not to our appetite but to the LORD. The church recovers this in valiant, self-spending devotion to Christ the greater David.
roots_summary: From Hebrew gibborim, mighty ones, the title of the valiant warriors gathered to David the king.
roots_lines: Hebrew gibbor (plural gibborim) is a man of valour, from gabar, to prevail.
"The three" were the highest rank, men of singular and lonely feats of war.
"The thirty" formed the larger fellowship of named captains under David.
Adullam's cave was the gathering-place where the distressed first rallied to David (1 Sam 22:2).
The water of Bethlehem, poured out, became a memorial of valour offered unto the LORD.
usage: David's mighty men brake through the Philistine host merely to fetch their king a drink of water.
The roll of David's mighty men closes with Uriah the Hittite, whose name carries a later grief.
Among David's mighty men Benaiah was renowned for slaying a lion in a pit in the time of snow.

etymology: Hebrew Zilpah, of uncertain meaning, perhaps "a trickling" or "fragrant dropping"; the handmaid of Leah given to Jacob.
biblical_def: Zilpah was the handmaid whom Laban gave to his daughter Leah at her marriage (Gen 29:24), and who afterward became a secondary wife to Jacob. When Leah saw that she had left bearing, she took Zilpah her maid and gave her to Jacob to wife; and Zilpah bare Jacob two sons, Gad and Asher (Gen 30:9-13). At Gad's birth Leah said, "A troop cometh", and at Asher's, "Happy am I, for the daughters will call me blessed" (Gen 30:13). These two sons became fathers of two of the twelve tribes of Israel, so that Zilpah, though a bondwoman, stands within the patriarchal household as mother of a quarter part of the tribes through which the covenant promises ran. The Scripture records her without disguising the disorder of the household, the rivalry of Leah and Rachel, the giving of handmaids, the contention for children, for the polygamy of the patriarchs was permitted in that age but never approved as the creation ordinance; from the beginning it was one man and one woman (Gen 2:24; Matt 19:4-6). Yet through this tangled house God sovereignly raised up the tribes of Israel and kept His promise to Abraham. This dictionary confesses that God's purposes run on through the weakness and sin of His people, that He honours even the bondwoman by making her a mother in Israel, and that the wisdom of God is glorified in bringing His covenant to pass through such imperfect vessels.
webster_summary: Leah's handmaid, given to Jacob as a wife, who bore Gad and Asher. Through her two of the twelve tribes of Israel arose within the patriarchal household.
webster_full: ZILPAH, noun. The handmaid of Leah, given by her to Jacob, and mother of Gad and Asher.
"And Zilpah Leah's maid bare Jacob a son" (Gen 30:10).
Her place in the household sprang from Leah's rivalry with Rachel for children.
She bore two sons who became fathers of two tribes of Israel.
The closing sense: a bondwoman made a mother in Israel by the sovereign purpose of God.
scriptures: And Laban gave unto his daughter Leah Zilpah his maid for an handmaid.
Gen 30:9
When Leah saw that she had left bearing, she took Zilpah her maid, and gave her Jacob to wife.
And Zilpah Leah's maid bare Jacob a son.
And Leah said, Happy am I, for the daughters will call me blessed: and she called his name Asher.
corruption_summary: Zilpah faces no modern redefinition; her account recovers the truth that God works His covenant through a disordered house without approving its sin.
corruption_paragraphs: The household of Jacob, with its two wives and two handmaids and their striving for children, is recorded with unflinching honesty. Scripture does not hide that the giving of Zilpah and Bilhah arose from rivalry and from a custom that fell short of the creation pattern of one man and one woman. The narrative reports without commending; the bitterness between Leah and Rachel is the fruit of departing from God's first ordinance of marriage.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sovereignty of God over the tangled affairs of His people. He did not require the polygamy, yet He overruled it, raising the tribes of Israel even from the handmaids' sons. Zilpah, a bondwoman, became a mother in Israel, a witness that the covenant advances by grace and not by the worthiness of the vessels through which it passes.
roots_summary: From Hebrew Zilpah, the name of Leah's handmaid who became mother of Gad and Asher.
roots_lines: Hebrew Zilpah is of uncertain sense, perhaps "a trickling" or "fragrant dropping."
She was first Leah's shiphchah, a maidservant given at marriage by Laban.
Given "to wife" to Jacob, she held the place of a secondary or concubine-wife.
Gad, "a troop," and Asher, "happy," were her two sons (Gen 30:11-13).
Her two sons stand among the twelve patriarchs of the tribes of Israel.
usage: Zilpah bare Gad and Asher to Jacob, and so a quarter of the tribes sprang from Leah's handmaid.
The naming of Zilpah's sons reflects Leah's contention with Rachel for honour in the house.
Though only a handmaid, Zilpah is numbered among the mothers of Israel by the purpose of God.

etymology: Hebrew Yisra'el, "he striveth with God" or "God striveth," from sarah, to strive or have power, and el, God; the new name given to Jacob.
biblical_def: The covenant name given to Jacob by God at Peniel, when Jacob wrestled with the Angel of the LORD until the breaking of the day and would not let Him go except He blessed him. The man said, "Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed" (Gen 32:28). Jacob called the name of the place Peniel, "for I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved" (Gen 32:30). The name was confirmed to him again at Bethel: "Thy name is Jacob: thy name shall not be called any more Jacob, but Israel shall be thy name" (Gen 35:10). The name passed from the man to the people; the twelve tribes that sprang from his loins are "the children of Israel," and the nation bears his new name as the chosen and covenant people of God. It signifies not the supplanter's craft of "Jacob" but the prevailing power of one who, made weak in the thigh, clung to God in prayer and prevailed by laying hold of His promise. This dictionary confesses that the true Israel is the people of faith, for they are not all Israel which are of Israel (Rom 9:6), and that the church of believing Jew and Gentile is the Israel of God (Gal 6:16), grafted into the covenant and made to prevail not by their strength but by clinging to the same God who blessed Jacob at the brook.
webster_summary: The covenant name given to Jacob at Peniel after he wrestled with God and prevailed. It became the name of the chosen people, the twelve tribes and the church of faith.
webster_full: ISRAEL, noun. The name given to Jacob at Peniel, signifying "he hath power with God," and borne by his descendants.
"Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed" (Gen 32:28).
It was given at the wrestling, where Jacob clung to God in prayer and would not let Him go.
It passed from the man to the nation, the twelve tribes called the children of Israel.
The closing sense: the true Israel is the covenant people of faith, the Israel of God.
scriptures: And he said, Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed.
And God said unto him, Thy name is Jacob: thy name shall not be called any more Jacob, but Israel shall be thy name: and he called his name Israel.
Rom 9:6
Not as though the word of God hath taken none effect. For they are not all Israel, which are of Israel.
Gal 6:16
And as many as walk according to this rule, peace be on them, and mercy, and upon the Israel of God.
corruption_summary: The name Israel faces no postmodern redefinition; it recovers the truth that the covenant people are constituted by God's naming and by prevailing faith.
corruption_paragraphs: The renaming at Peniel marks a turning in Jacob's life from craft to faith. "Jacob" recalled the heel-grasper who supplanted his brother and bargained for blessing; "Israel" declares one who, crippled in the wrestling, prevailed by clinging to God and pleading His promise. The new name is no reward for cunning but the seal of a faith that holds fast to God even when overmatched, and the lameness he carried away taught him that he prevailed only as he was first made weak.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that membership in Israel was never merely a matter of natural descent. The apostle teaches that they are not all Israel which are of Israel, and that the believing remnant, with the Gentiles grafted in, is the Israel of God. The covenant name belongs in its fulness to the people of faith, who prevail with God as Jacob did, by laying hold of His grace in Christ.
roots_summary: From Hebrew Yisra'el, "he striveth with God," the name given to Jacob when he prevailed at Peniel.
roots_lines: Hebrew Yisra'el joins sarah, to strive or prevail, with el, God.
Peniel, "the face of God," named the place of the wrestling (Gen 32:30).
The name replaced Ya'aqob, "he taketh by the heel" or "supplanter."
"As a prince hast thou power" renders the sense of striving and prevailing with God.
The plural "children of Israel" became the standing name of the covenant nation.
usage: At Peniel the wrestling Angel changed his name from Jacob to Israel, for he had prevailed.
The whole nation bears the patriarch's new name, the children of Israel, God's chosen people.
Paul teaches that the true Israel is the people of faith, not all who descend from Israel by blood.

etymology: Hebrew Shephelah, "the lowland" or "low country," from shaphel, to be low; the foothills between the coastal plain and the highlands of Judah.
biblical_def: The Shephelah is the region of low rolling foothills that lies between the maritime plain of Philistia on the west and the high central mountains of Judah on the east, rendered in the King James Version as "the vale," "the valley," or "the low country" (Josh 10:40; 11:16; 15:33). It was a fertile and well-watered land of grain and sycomore trees; Solomon "made cedars to be as the sycomore trees that are in the vale, for abundance" (1 Kings 10:27). Yet its greater note in Scripture is military, for it was the contested borderland and the fortress region guarding the approaches to the Judean hill country. Its cities, Lachish, Azekah, Beth-shemesh, Libnah, and others named in Joshua 15, were the strongholds that Judah held and lost and held again against the Philistines, the Assyrians, and the Babylonians. It was in the valley of Elah within the Shephelah that David met Goliath of Gath (1 Sam 17:2). Because it lay open between two peoples and powers, the Shephelah was perpetually fought over, a frontier where the strength of Judah was tested. This dictionary confesses that the LORD gave Israel the land, hills and valleys alike, as the inheritance of His covenant, and that the borderlands no less than the heights were held by His hand, who fought for His people and delivered the giant of the Philistines into the hand of a shepherd boy.
webster_summary: The lowland foothills between the coastal plain and the Judean highlands, with fortress cities like Lachish and Azekah. A fertile but perpetually contested borderland of Judah.
webster_full: SHEPHELAH, noun. The low country or foothills lying between the coastal plain and the mountains of Judah.
"And the valley, Eshtaol, and Zoreah, and Ashnah" (Josh 15:33), among its many border cities.
Its place required of Judah constant guarding, for it lay open between Philistia and the highlands.
It held the fortress cities of Lachish, Azekah, and Beth-shemesh, and the valley of Elah.
The closing sense: a contested frontier of the inheritance, given and kept by the LORD's hand.
scriptures: Josh 10:40

So Joshua smote all the country of the hills, and of the south, and of the vale, and of the springs, and all their kings: he left none remaining, but utterly destroyed all that breathed, as the LORD God of Israel commanded.
Josh 15:33
And in the valley, Eshtaol, and Zoreah, and Ashnah.
And Saul and the men of Israel were gathered together, and pitched by the valley of Elah, and set the battle in array against the Philistines.
1 Kings 10:27
And the king made silver to be in Jerusalem as stones, and cedars made he to be as the sycomore trees that are in the vale, for abundance.
corruption_summary: The Shephelah faces no postmodern redefinition; its history recovers the truth that the LORD gave and guarded the whole inheritance of His people, valleys as well as heights.
corruption_paragraphs: The Shephelah was the soft underbelly of Judah, the open country where invading armies pressed inward toward Jerusalem. For this reason its towns were fortified and refortified, and its fields became battlegrounds again and again. Lachish, its chief stronghold, was besieged and taken by the Assyrian Sennacherib and later by the Babylonians, and the prophets reckoned its fall as a sign of judgment upon the whole land.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the inheritance God gave to Israel was a real land with real borders to be kept by faith and obedience. The Shephelah teaches that the frontiers of the covenant people were never secured by their own strength alone; it was in its valley of Elah that the LORD delivered the Philistine champion into the hand of David, that all the earth might know there is a God in Israel.
roots_summary: From Hebrew Shephelah, "the lowland," from shaphel, to be low; the foothills of western Judah.
roots_lines: Hebrew Shephelah comes from shaphel, to be low or brought down.
The KJV renders it "the vale," "the valley," or "the low country."
It lay between the negeb and coastal plain westward and the hill country eastward.
Lachish, Azekah, and Beth-shemesh were among its chief fortress cities.
The valley of Elah within it was the field of David's combat with Goliath.
usage: The fortress cities of the Shephelah guarded the western approaches to the Judean highlands.
David slew Goliath in the valley of Elah, set within the contested borderland of the Shephelah.
Sennacherib's siege of Lachish struck at the chief stronghold of the Shephelah of Judah.

etymology: Rendering Hebrew meshiach YHWH, the anointed of the LORD, from mashach, to anoint with oil; the title of one set apart by anointing to office under God.
biblical_def: The title borne by the king whom God had set apart by the holy anointing oil, marking him as sacrosanct, not to be touched or harmed by the hand of man. When David twice had Saul, his persecutor, delivered into his power, he would not stretch out his hand, saying, "The LORD forbid that I should do this thing unto my master, the LORD's anointed, to stretch forth mine hand against him, seeing he is the anointed of the LORD" (1 Sam 24:6). Again David charged Abishai, "Who can stretch forth his hand against the LORD's anointed, and be guiltless?" (1 Sam 26:9). Thus even a wicked king, while he yet held the office, was reverenced for the sake of the One who had anointed him; the office was God's, and to assault the anointed was to despise God's appointment. The phrase looks beyond Saul and David to the great Anointed of whom the kings were but shadows. The Psalmist foretells the raging of kings "against the LORD, and against his anointed" (Psa 2:2), and the apostles apply this directly to the gathering of Herod and Pilate against the holy child Jesus, "whom thou hast anointed" (Acts 4:26-27). The Hebrew mashiach is the very word Messiah, the Christ. This dictionary confesses that all the anointed kings of Israel pointed forward to Jesus Christ, the true and final Anointed, anointed not with oil but with the Holy Ghost without measure, the King whom God has set upon His holy hill of Zion.
webster_summary: The title of the king set apart by God's anointing, held sacrosanct as in David's sparing of Saul. The office pointed forward to Christ, the true Anointed of the LORD.
webster_full: THE LORD'S ANOINTED, noun. One set apart by the holy anointing to royal office under God, and so accounted sacred.
"Who can stretch forth his hand against the LORD's anointed, and be guiltless?" (1 Sam 26:9).
The title required that even an enemy honour the office God had conferred by anointing.
It forbids the lifting of a hand against him whom the LORD has set apart, for the office is God's.
The closing sense: a shadow fulfilled in Christ, the Messiah, the true Anointed of the LORD.
scriptures: And he said unto his men, The LORD forbid that I should do this thing unto my master, the LORD's anointed, to stretch forth mine hand against him, seeing he is the anointed of the LORD.
And David said to Abishai, Destroy him not: for who can stretch forth his hand against the LORD's anointed, and be guiltless?
Psa 2:2
The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD, and against his anointed, saying,
Acts 4:27
For of a truth against thy holy child Jesus, whom thou hast anointed, both Herod, and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles, and the people of Israel, were gathered together,
corruption_summary: The title faces no postmodern redefinition; it recovers the truth that the anointing is God's appointment, fulfilled at last in Christ the Messiah.
corruption_paragraphs: David's refusal to harm Saul is one of the great instances of faith honouring God's appointment above its own advantage. Saul was a fallen and murderous king, and the cave at En-gedi offered David a quick deliverance; yet David trembled to touch the anointed of the LORD, choosing to wait upon God to remove Saul in His own time rather than to seize the crown by a guilty stroke. The reverence was not for Saul the man but for the office God had set upon him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the Godward reading of the title. The anointed king was a type, and the second Psalm gathers all the figures into one: the rulers rage against the LORD and against His anointed. The apostles confess that this anointed is Jesus, the Christ, the very Messiah; and the dictionary owns Him as the true Anointed, Prophet, Priest, and King, whom no enemy could finally touch and whom God has exalted to His right hand.
roots_summary: From Hebrew meshiach, the anointed one, from mashach, to anoint; the source of the words Messiah and Christ.
roots_lines: Hebrew mashach means to anoint with oil, setting a person apart to office.
Mashiach, the anointed one, is the word from which "Messiah" comes.
The Greek Christos, "Christ," renders the same idea of the Anointed.
Kings, priests, and prophets were each anointed, but the king especially bore this title.
The anointing oil signified the setting apart and, in Christ, the Spirit without measure.
usage: David would not lift his hand against Saul, for he was the LORD's anointed.
The second Psalm warns the kings of the earth who set themselves against the LORD's anointed.
Every anointed king of Israel was a shadow of Christ, the true and final LORD's anointed.
